newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton seen triumphant in summit with Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seen triumphant in summit with Yeltsin.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin have given their partnership a boost with a successful summit, although the Kremlin chief may find he has lost a crucial battle over NATO enlargement.

A range of agreements covering issues from Russia's economic place on the world stage to a pledge of further cuts in nuclear weapons sealed the post-Cold War relationship the two leaders have worked hard to build. It was their 11th meeting.

Although they publicly agreed to differ on NATO enlargement, Yeltsin appeared to have made concessions which enraged his critics at home but delighted the Western alliance and former Soviet bloc states which are now clamouring to join.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said after the two-day summit which ended on Friday that Clinton had made "history in Helsinki".
"We have opened a new stage of American-Russian relations," Yeltsin enthusiastically agreed.

The meeting was dubbed the "summit of the invalids", with Clinton confined to a wheelchair following a leg injury and Yeltsin still recovering from heart surgery and illness. Clinton flew home on Friday, while Yeltsin was staying until Saturday.
Both sides were careful to portray the summit as an even-handed affair with compromises on both sides.
Yeltsin had to avoid looking weak in front of his communist and nationalist critics at home, while Clinton wanted to stress the West's real intention of a partnership with Russia.
In Moscow, Russian Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov was scathing and said Moscow had been dealt a "crushing defeat".

"The Helsinki agreements are Russia's Versailles," he said. It was a reference to the Versailles Treaty of 1919 which ended World War One and set humiliating conditions for Germany, the loser. It also helped create the conditions for Adolf Hitler to come to power.
Before the meeting, the Kremlin blasted NATO enlargement as a threat to Russia's security and suggested there could be a major row at the summit.
Yeltsin, though, took a more conciliatory approach -- despite repeating Russia's longstanding opposition to the 16-nation alliance's expansion plans.

First, he committed himself in Helsinki to cutting out the tough anti-NATO rhetoric that has worried governments across central and eastern Europe by promising with Clinton to "minimise the consequences of this disagreement".

Second, Yeltsin formally dropped Moscow's demand that a charter defining a new relationship between NATO and Russia should be legally binding, accepting instead that it would be signed by NATO leaders and therefore be politically binding.

In return, Clinton promised to continue work on the charter, repeated some existing NATO assurances on the deployment of troops and nuclear weapons, and then firmly pledged that enlargement would go ahead on schedule.

Moreover, Clinton said the new NATO-Russia charter would give Moscow a "voice but not a veto" in European security and that new members of the alliance would not in any sense be "second class citizens" enjoying less protection than others.
Eastern European countries, worried that Russia could force a deal with the West that would leave them out in the cold, welcomed this reassurance with relief.

While Clinton was careful not to appear triumphant, Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski -- whose country expects to be among the first invited to join NATO at an alliance summit in July -- put it more bluntly in Warsaw.
"I think that in this basic question...Russia has agreed on the expansion of NATO," he said.
In Brussels, the alliance hailed the outcome of the summit as a major step towards a more secure and peaceful Europe.
Yeltsin and Clinton also resolved a long-running dispute over missile defences and held out the prospect of more cuts in their nuclear arsenals.
On economic matters, Clinton promised to try to get Russia into the Paris Club of government creditors this year and into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) next year.

The leaders also agreed that Russia would have an increased role in the Group of Seven (G7) club of rich industrialised nations. In exchange, Yeltsin promised to reform Russia's barely functioning tax regime and to crack down on corruption and organised crime.
